cards.title: The distance choice
cards.body: A shot size is how much of a person and a place you allow inside the frame. An extreme wide shot makes a figure tiny so the world feels larger than the character.

cards.title: Wide context
cards.body: A wide shot still shows the full room or street, and the person is readable from head to toe. Use it when the location is part of the pressure on the character.

cards.title: Full body
cards.body: A full shot fits the whole body with a modest margin above the head and below the feet. You can read posture, costume, and the first step of a walk.

cards.title: Medium range
cards.body: A medium frame usually runs from the head toward the waist or knees. Hands enter the story, and the face is close enough to catch a decision.

cards.title: Close and closer
cards.body: A close-up fills the frame with a face. An extreme close-up keeps only eyes or a mouth, so a blink can become the whole event. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Pick with a reason
cards.body: Choose the size that matches the information the audience needs in that second. If the room matters, stay wide. If a lie matters, come in close.

quiz.prompt: Which framing makes the place feel larger than the person?
quiz.why: An extreme wide shot shrinks the figure inside a large world.

quiz.prompt: A full shot is mainly useful because it shows
quiz.why: Head-to-toe framing lets posture and costume read clearly.

quiz.prompt: When should you move closer?
options: When a small change in the face is the point
When you want more parking lot
quiz.why: Closer frames trade location for expression and detail.

cards.title: Eye level
cards.body: An eye-level camera meets the person as a peer. It feels neutral, which is useful when you want the audience to judge the moment without being pushed.

cards.title: Low angle
cards.body: A low angle looks up. The horizon drops, the figure grows, and the person can feel stronger, taller, or more threatening even if the dialogue stays quiet.

cards.title: High angle
cards.body: A high angle looks down. The horizon rises and the person can feel smaller, watched, or stuck, especially if the floor fills the lower frame. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Dutch tilt
cards.body: A Dutch angle rolls the horizon off level. The place feels uneasy. Use it sparingly, because a tilt with no story reason just looks like a mistake.

cards.title: Over the shoulder
cards.body: An over-the-shoulder angle puts a nearer shoulder in the foreground and the other person beyond it. The audience sits inside the conversation. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Match the power
cards.body: Ask who holds the moment before you pick the height. Heroes, bullies, and frightened people should not all be photographed from the same polite height. Keep a one-line note so you can find the pattern again tomorrow.

quiz.prompt: A low angle tends to make a person feel
quiz.why: Looking up enlarges the figure and drops the horizon.

quiz.prompt: A Dutch angle is a tilt of the
quiz.why: The horizon leaves level, which makes the frame feel unstable.

quiz.prompt: Over-the-shoulder framing places the audience
options: Inside one person's view of another
quiz.why: The foreground shoulder puts us in the conversation.

cards.title: The grid
cards.body: Imagine the frame split into thirds, both across and down. The four crossings are calm places to rest an eye, a face, or a horizon. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: Lead room
cards.body: If a person looks or walks to the right, leave open space on that side. The empty area is lead room, and it lets the look have somewhere to go.

cards.title: Headroom
cards.body: Headroom is the space above the hair. Too much and the person sinks. Too little and the frame feels cramped. Match it to how close you are.

cards.title: Horizon line
cards.body: A horizon on the lower third gives the sky the story. A horizon on the upper third gives the ground the story. The center is calm and formal.

cards.title: Break it on purpose
cards.body: Center a face when the moment is symmetrical, formal, or trapped. Breaking the thirds works when you can say why, not when you forgot the grid.

cards.title: Move, then settle
cards.body: During a pan the subject can cross the center. When the camera settles, give the look room again so the frame feels finished rather than caught mid-step.

quiz.prompt: Lead room belongs
options: Behind the direction of the look
In front of the direction of the look
quiz.why: Open space in front of a look gives the gaze somewhere to travel.

quiz.prompt: A low horizon emphasizes the
quiz.why: Putting the horizon low hands most of the frame to the sky.

quiz.prompt: Centering a subject is useful when the moment is
quiz.why: A centered face can feel deliberate, trapped, or ceremonial.

cards.title: Three distances
cards.body: A frame with a foreground, a subject, and a background feels deeper than a flat wall. Even a doorframe or a shoulder can be the near layer.

cards.title: Foreground as a frame
cards.body: A dark doorway, a plant, or a shoulder at the edge tells the eye where to enter. It also hides a little, which makes the reveal feel earned.

cards.title: Separation
cards.body: If the subject and the wall share the same brightness, they melt together. A rim of light or a shift in focus pulls the person off the background.

cards.title: Planes of action
cards.body: Let an extra cross the foreground while the main action stays in the middle. The passing shape adds life without stealing the sentence being spoken. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Depth with lenses
cards.body: A longer lens stacks layers so a street looks compressed. A wider lens stretches the gap between a hand in front and a door behind. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Do not clutter
cards.body: Depth is not a pile of objects. One clear near shape, one subject, and one readable background are enough for the eye to travel. Keep a one-line note so you can find the pattern again tomorrow.

quiz.prompt: A simple deep frame usually has
quiz.why: Three distances give the eye a path into the shot.

quiz.prompt: A longer lens tends to make distances look
quiz.why: Telephoto stacking squeezes the space between layers.

quiz.prompt: Foreground shapes help when they
options: Guide the eye and add a near layer
quiz.why: A partial near shape frames the subject instead of burying it.

cards.title: Focal length
cards.body: Focal length describes how wide or narrow the lens sees. A short lens takes in more of the room. A long lens reaches a smaller slice from farther away.

cards.title: Wide feeling
cards.body: Wide lenses exaggerate distance. A hand toward the lens looks large, and a hallway seems to stretch. That stretch can feel energetic or unsettling. Look for the opposite choice in the following scene and compare the feeling.

cards.title: Long feeling
cards.body: Long lenses flatten faces gently and pile the background close behind the subject. Crowds, traffic, and hills feel nearer than a walk would suggest. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Portrait range
cards.body: A moderate telephoto is a common portrait choice because the face stays natural and the background softens. You are not stuck with it, but it is a kind default.

cards.title: Focus falloff
cards.body: Wider lenses keep more of the set sharp. Longer lenses, opened up, throw the background into blur so a face can separate from a busy street.

cards.title: Choose the distance too
cards.body: The same framing from a different distance is a different picture. Walk closer with a wide lens or step back with a long lens and watch the room change.

quiz.prompt: A short focal length sees
quiz.why: Wide lenses include more of the surroundings.

quiz.prompt: Long lenses often make the background feel
quiz.why: Telephoto compression piles distant layers behind the subject.

quiz.prompt: To change the feel without changing the crop, you can
options: Change lens and camera distance together
quiz.why: Matching the crop from a new distance changes perspective.

cards.title: Motivation
cards.body: Move the camera when the story moves: a look, a walk, a reveal, or a change in attention. A drift with no reason feels like the tripod was bored.

cards.title: Pan and tilt
cards.body: A pan turns left or right. A tilt tips up or down. Lead the subject a little so they do not bump the edge the moment they start walking.

cards.title: Dolly and track
cards.body: A dolly rolls the whole camera nearer, farther, or alongside. Unlike a zoom, the perspective changes because the camera actually travels. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Zoom
cards.body: A zoom changes focal length without moving the camera. The world stretches or stacks, but you do not travel through the room. Use it when the decision is optical.

cards.title: Handheld
cards.body: Handheld movement adds breath and urgency. Keep the horizon mostly level unless the scene is truly chaotic, and give the operator a path so the shake stays intentional.

cards.title: Start and stop
cards.body: Ease into a move and ease out. A hard start looks like a mistake. Hold a beat at the end so the audience can read the new frame before the cut.

quiz.prompt: A dolly differs from a zoom because the camera
quiz.why: Travel changes perspective. A zoom only changes focal length.

quiz.prompt: A pan is a turn
quiz.why: Pan is the horizontal swivel.

quiz.prompt: A move feels finished when you
options: Hold a readable frame at the end
quiz.why: A short hold lets the new composition land.

cards.title: Key light
cards.body: The key is the main light that explains the shape of a face. Place it off to one side so a cheek, a nose, and an eye socket get different brightness.

cards.title: Fill light
cards.body: Fill opens the shadow side just enough to keep detail. If fill equals the key, the face goes flat. If fill is absent, the mood gets stark.

cards.title: Back light
cards.body: A back light, or rim, traces hair and shoulder so the person separates from a dark wall. It is often the difference between a portrait and a silhouette by accident.

cards.title: Ratios
cards.body: Think of the relationship, not a shopping list of lamps. A strong key and weak fill feels dramatic. A closer match feels open, calm, or documentary.

cards.title: One source first
cards.body: Start with the key alone and look. Add fill only if the shadow hides a story you still need. Add a rim if the person disappears into the set.

cards.title: Eye light
cards.body: A small reflection in the eyes keeps a face alive. It can be the key itself. If the eyes go dead, nudge a soft source until a tiny catchlight appears.

quiz.prompt: The key light is
options: The main light shaping the face
quiz.why: The key is the primary modeling light.

quiz.prompt: Fill is used to
options: Open shadows without flattening them completely
quiz.why: Fill controls how much shadow detail remains.

quiz.prompt: A rim light helps the subject
quiz.why: The edge light traces hair and shoulder against the set.

cards.title: Hard light
cards.body: A small, distant source throws a hard shadow with a crisp edge. Noon sun and a bare bulb are hard. The shadow becomes a graphic shape in the frame.

cards.title: Soft light
cards.body: A large source relative to the face wraps around cheeks and softens the shadow line. Overcast sky, a big window, or a diffused lamp all behave this way.

cards.title: Distance and size
cards.body: Moving a soft source closer makes it relatively larger and even softer. Backing it away makes it harder. Size is about the source compared with the subject.

cards.title: Shadow story
cards.body: Hard light can feel harsh, comic, or dangerous. Soft light can feel intimate, overcast, or kind. Neither is morally better. Match the edge to the scene.

cards.title: Mixed edges
cards.body: A hard key and a soft fill is a classic mix. The bright side has shape, and the shadow side still holds a gentle detail instead of a black hole.

cards.title: Watch the nose
cards.body: On a face, the nose shadow tells you the edge quality immediately. If that shadow is a sharp stripe, you are in hard light even if the room looks pretty.

quiz.prompt: Hard light is associated with a shadow that is
quiz.why: A small source makes a defined shadow edge.

quiz.prompt: A source becomes softer when it is
quiz.why: A larger apparent source wraps the face.

quiz.prompt: The nose shadow is a quick test of
quiz.why: A sharp nose shadow means the key is hard.

cards.title: Color temperature
cards.body: Warm light leans amber, like a household lamp or sunset. Cool light leans blue, like shade, moonlight in movies, or a north window at noon. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: Contrast of color
cards.body: A warm face against a cool window feels richer than a frame where every surface shares one color. The difference guides the eye without a louder performance.

cards.title: Motivation
cards.body: If the story lamp is tungsten, let the key be warm. If the night outside is the source, let the edge go cool. The audience believes light that has a visible cause.

cards.title: Skin
cards.body: Faces usually want a color you would still call skin. You can warm them, but a strong green or heavy blue on skin needs a reason or it feels like a mistake.

cards.title: Time of day
cards.body: Late sun is warm and low. Open shade is cooler. Mixing them in one room, with sun on the table and shade on the wall, sells the hour.

cards.title: Grade later, plan now
cards.body: You can push color in the finish, but the separation has to be photographed. If everything is the same gray, no grade will invent a window that was never there.

quiz.prompt: Household lamps are usually described as
quiz.why: Tungsten and many practical lamps read amber.

quiz.prompt: A warm face against a cool window creates
quiz.why: Opposite colors separate subject and setting.

quiz.prompt: Skin color usually needs
options: A reason if it leaves a believable range
quiz.why: Odd skin color should be motivated, not accidental.

cards.title: Contrast
cards.body: Contrast is the gap between the bright side and the shadow side. A small gap feels open and even. A large gap feels dramatic, late, or secretive.

cards.title: High contrast
cards.body: Deep shadows and bright edges can suggest night, danger, or a harsh sun. Protect one detail you still need, such as the eyes, so the face does not vanish.

cards.title: Low contrast
cards.body: When shadows stay readable, the scene can feel like daytime interior, a gentle memory, or a calm conversation. The set remains visible behind the person. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Ratio in practice
cards.body: You do not need a meter to begin. Squint. If the shadow cheek disappears, contrast is high. If both cheeks look similar, contrast is low. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Background too
cards.body: A bright window behind a dark face is also contrast. Expose with a choice: keep the face and let the window bloom, or keep the view and let the face fall.

cards.title: Change it in the scene
cards.body: Contrast can shift when a character steps from a hallway into a lamp. That change is a story beat, not a continuity error, if you planned the geography.

quiz.prompt: High contrast means the bright-to-shadow gap is
quiz.why: A big gap between highlight and shadow is high contrast.

quiz.prompt: Squinting helps you judge whether
quiz.why: If the shadow cheek vanishes when you squint, contrast is strong.

quiz.prompt: A bright window behind a person forces a choice about
quiz.why: You choose face detail or the view outside.

cards.title: Motivated light
cards.body: Motivated light pretends to come from a source the audience can believe: a window, a lamp, a sign, a fireplace, or the open sky. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: The practical
cards.body: A practical is a lamp that appears in the frame. It may be too weak to light the face alone, so a hidden source can imitate it from the same direction.

cards.title: Direction first
cards.body: Before you add brightness, point the light from the story source. A pretty face lit from the wrong side of a visible window feels false even if the exposure is nice.

cards.title: Cheating
cards.body: You may cheat the source a little toward camera so eyes stay alive. Keep the cheat on the same side as the window or lamp so the logic holds.

cards.title: Offscreen sources
cards.body: A streetlamp just out of frame can still motivate a rim. Show a hint of it, or a glow on the wall, so the audience knows the light has a home.

cards.title: When style breaks logic
cards.body: A musical number or a dream can use light that no room would make. Signal that freedom with the rest of the style so it feels chosen.

quiz.prompt: Motivated light appears to come from
options: A source the story can believe
A random color with no cause
quiz.why: Windows, lamps, and sky give light a cause.

quiz.prompt: A practical is
options: A lamp seen in the frame
quiz.why: Practicals are visible fixtures in the set.

quiz.prompt: A small cheat toward camera is fair if you
options: Keep it on the source's side
quiz.why: The direction should still agree with the visible source.

cards.title: Mood inventory
cards.body: Light can feel safe, lonely, festive, sick, holy, or cheap. Pick one word before you place a lamp, then refuse choices that fight that word. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: Direction and mood
cards.body: Light from below can feel eerie because sunlight rarely does that. Light from a high side window can feel like late afternoon even without a clock.

cards.title: Color and mood
cards.body: Amber pools feel domestic. Cyan edges feel nocturnal or clinical. A single saturated color in a otherwise quiet frame becomes the mood all by itself. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Contrast and mood
cards.body: Open shadows feel honest or daytime. Crushed shadows feel secret, night, or menace. The same dialogue changes temperature when the gap between cheeks changes. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Movement of light
cards.body: A passing headlight, a flickering sign, or a door opening can change mood inside the shot. Let the change happen for a story reason, then settle.

cards.title: Consistency
cards.body: Once a scene promises a mood, keep it through the coverage. A sudden flat wide shot in a moody close-up scene breaks the spell harder than a small continuity slip.

quiz.prompt: A useful first step for mood is to
options: Pick a word and light toward it
quiz.why: One clear mood word steers direction, color, and contrast.

quiz.prompt: Light from below often feels odd because
options: Natural sun rarely comes from there
quiz.why: Underlighting fights everyday experience, so it feels uncanny.

quiz.prompt: Coverage should
quiz.why: The wide shot and the close-up should belong to the same world.

cards.title: A cut is a join
cards.body: A cut replaces one shot with another at a chosen frame. The audience reads the join as a thought: meanwhile, therefore, later, or closer. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: Why cut
cards.body: Cut to answer a question the previous shot raised, or to ask a new one. If the new shot adds nothing, the cut feels like a blink for its own sake.

cards.title: Shot, reverse, shot
cards.body: A simple conversation pattern shows one person, then the other, then back. The rhythm can speed up as the argument tightens. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Cut on action
cards.body: If a hand reaches and the next shot continues the reach, the eye follows the motion and forgives the join. Action is a bridge. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Hold for the reaction
cards.body: Sometimes the better cut stays on the listener. The line is in the sound, and the story is in the face that receives it. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Do not rescue
cards.body: Editing can shape a performance, but it cannot invent an angle you never filmed. Coverage is a promise you make on set for the bench later.

quiz.prompt: A cut is best when the new shot
options: Adds a new piece of story information
Repeats the same frame for no reason
quiz.why: Each join should change what the audience knows or feels.

quiz.prompt: Cutting on action helps because
quiz.why: Continuing movement carries the eye across the cut.

quiz.prompt: A reaction shot is useful when
options: The listener's face is the story
quiz.why: The response can matter more than the speaker's mouth.

cards.title: Screen direction
cards.body: If a person walks left to right, the next shot should keep that direction unless you show a turn. A sudden flip feels like they changed their mind without a scene.

cards.title: Eyelines
cards.body: When two people talk, their looks should meet. If both look off to the same side, they seem to be staring past each other into different rooms.

cards.title: The line
cards.body: Imagine a line through the two people. Keep the camera on one side of it and the left-right relationship stays stable. Cross it only with a moving shot that explains the cross.

cards.title: Props and hands
cards.body: A glass in the right hand should not jump to the left hand after a cut. Small prop jumps are loud because the audience was watching the gesture.

cards.title: Matching action
cards.body: Start the next shot a little before the move finishes so you can choose a frame where the hands agree. Overlap is a gift from set to the edit.

cards.title: When to break
cards.body: A dream, a panic, or a comic double take can break continuity on purpose. The break should feel like style, not like a missed note in an otherwise careful scene.

quiz.prompt: Screen direction should stay consistent unless you
options: Show a turn or a motivated crossing
quiz.why: An unexplained flip reads as a mistake.

quiz.prompt: Eyelines in a conversation should
options: Both aim at the same empty side
quiz.why: Opposite looks sell that the people see one another.

quiz.prompt: The imaginary line helps you keep
quiz.why: Staying on one side of the line preserves geography.

cards.title: Shot length
cards.body: Rhythm is the pattern of how long shots last. A string of short shots feels urgent. A long hold feels like waiting, dread, or calm. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: Accent
cards.body: Not every cut should be the same length. A sudden short shot after three long ones is an accent, like a drummer leaving a gap and then striking.

cards.title: Dialogue rhythm
cards.body: People rarely talk in equal bars. Let some lines finish in the shot and some land on the listener. The unevenness feels like speech, not a metronome.

cards.title: Breathing room
cards.body: After a revelation, a short hold lets the audience feel it. Cutting away instantly can look like you were afraid of the performance. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Music and cuts
cards.body: You may cut with the music or against it. With the beat feels planned and sometimes comic. Against the beat can feel tense or free. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Watch it mute
cards.body: Play the scene without sound. If the picture still has a pulse, the rhythm is really there. If it dies, the music was doing all the work.

quiz.prompt: A run of very short shots tends to feel
quiz.why: Frequent cuts raise the sense of speed.

quiz.prompt: An accent in editing is
options: A shot length that breaks the pattern
quiz.why: Changing the established duration makes a beat land.

quiz.prompt: Watching a cut mute helps you test
options: Whether the picture has its own pulse
quiz.why: If rhythm depends only on music, the picture is thin.

cards.title: What a montage is
cards.body: A montage is a chain of shots that collapses time. Training, travel, a season of work, or a relationship changing can pass in a minute of fragments.

cards.title: Progress
cards.body: Each fragment should show a change: a higher stack of papers, a longer run, a colder coat. If every shot repeats the same information, time does not feel like it moved.

cards.title: The unifying idea
cards.body: Hold the sequence together with one idea, one piece of music, or one repeated gesture. The audience should know what is being compressed. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Enter and exit
cards.body: Start the montage with a clear before, and land on a clear after. The last shot is the result the sequence was building. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Not a junk drawer
cards.body: Montage is not a place to hide shots you like but do not understand. If a shot does not change the state of the story, leave it out.

cards.title: Sound across it
cards.body: A continuous voice, song, or room tone can glue different days together. A hard silence between fragments makes them feel like separate scenes instead of one passage.

quiz.prompt: A montage mainly
quiz.why: Fragments stand in for a longer stretch of story time.

quiz.prompt: Each fragment should
quiz.why: Progress keeps the sequence moving.

quiz.prompt: The end of a montage should land on
quiz.why: The last image is the after that the chain earned.

cards.title: The straight cut
cards.body: Most joins should be straight cuts. They are invisible when the idea is clear. Fancy transitions are seasoning, not the meal. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: Dissolve
cards.body: A dissolve blends two images and often means time passing, memory, or a soft comparison. A dissolve in the middle of continuous action usually feels sleepy.

cards.title: Fade
cards.body: A fade to black can end a chapter or a day. A fade in can begin one. If you fade every scene, the film feels like it keeps falling asleep.

cards.title: Wipe and iris
cards.body: A wipe or an iris is graphic and often playful or old-fashioned. It announces itself. Use it when the story likes that announcement. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Match as transition
cards.body: A match cut joins two shots by a similar shape or motion. It compares ideas: a spinning plate becomes a planet, an eye becomes a tunnel.

cards.title: Sound lead
cards.body: Sometimes the next scene's sound arrives before the picture. That J-cut or L-cut is a transition too, and it can be smoother than any visual blend.

quiz.prompt: The default join should usually be a
quiz.why: Straight cuts carry most storytelling.

quiz.prompt: A dissolve often suggests
quiz.why: The blend reads as a softer passage of time or thought.

quiz.prompt: A match cut joins shots through
quiz.why: Visual rhyme links two ideas.

cards.title: Pace versus rhythm
cards.body: Rhythm is the local pattern of cuts. Pace is how fast the scene's information arrives. A scene can have lively rhythm and still take its time with the plot.

cards.title: Enter late
cards.body: Start the scene as close to the change as you can. Walking in, sitting down, and greeting can often be trimmed if the audience can infer them.

cards.title: Leave early
cards.body: Once the decision lands, you rarely need the goodbye. The next scene can answer the question. Lingering is a choice, not a duty. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Rise
cards.body: Let the scene tighten. Shorter lines, closer frames, and quicker reactions can build toward the turn. Then give the turn itself enough room to be seen.

cards.title: Air pockets
cards.body: A pause before a confession lets the audience lean in. Fill every gap and the confession arrives with no weight. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Scene against scene
cards.body: A fast scene after a slow one feels faster. Pace is relative. Build the film as a sequence of breaths, not as one speed from the first frame to the last.

quiz.prompt: Entering a scene late means you
quiz.why: Skip the approach when the audience can infer it.

quiz.prompt: A pause before an important line
quiz.why: Air lets the audience anticipate.

quiz.prompt: Pace is felt relative to
options: A single cut in isolation always
quiz.why: Contrast with neighboring scenes changes the feeling of speed.

cards.title: Diegetic
cards.body: Diegetic sound belongs to the world of the story. Footsteps, a radio in the kitchen, and dialogue the characters can hear are all inside that world.

cards.title: Non-diegetic
cards.body: A musical score the characters do not hear, or a narrator they cannot answer, sits outside the story world. The audience receives it as commentary. Look for the opposite choice in the following scene and compare the feeling.

cards.title: The border
cards.body: A song can start on a radio, which is diegetic, and then swell into a score, which is not. The handoff is a style choice if the moment of change is clear.

cards.title: Who hears it
cards.body: Ask who in the scene can hear the sound. If only the audience hears the low drone, it is a mood tool, not a truck outside.

cards.title: Point of hearing
cards.body: You can shift toward one character's ears: muffle the room, raise a tinnitus ring, duck the party. The mix becomes subjective without a visual effect. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Do not explain twice
cards.body: If the picture already shows the door slam, the sound should confirm it, not fight it. If you want surprise, let the sound arrive a fraction early or late on purpose.

quiz.prompt: Diegetic sound is heard
quiz.why: Characters could, in principle, hear diegetic sound.

quiz.prompt: A traditional score is usually
quiz.why: Characters typically do not hear the score.

quiz.prompt: Subjective hearing means the mix
quiz.why: Muffling or ringing can put us inside a head.

cards.title: What foley is
cards.body: Foley is performed sound for movement: steps, cloth, a cup set down, a key turned. It is recorded to picture so the gesture has a body.

cards.title: Why production sound is not enough
cards.body: Dialogue microphones are aimed at mouths, not shoes. The steps may be thin or full of other noise. Foley restores the gesture cleanly. Look for the opposite choice in the following scene and compare the feeling.

cards.title: Surface
cards.body: Wood, gravel, carpet, and wet stone should not share one generic thud. The surface tells the audience where the person is even in a tight close-up.

cards.title: Cloth
cards.body: A jacket shift when arms fold sells the costume. Too much cloth rustle fights the words. The art is choosing the gestures that matter. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Sync
cards.body: A step that lands a few frames late feels like a ghost. Line the impact up with the picture, then adjust level so it sits under the voice.

cards.title: Taste
cards.body: Not every tiny move needs a sound. Add the ones that carry story: the nervous glass, the careful step, the angry door. Leave the rest quiet.

quiz.prompt: Foley is mainly
options: Performed movement sound matched to picture
quiz.why: Artists perform steps and object handling to the image.

quiz.prompt: Shoe surfaces matter because they tell us
quiz.why: Gravel and carpet describe the place.

quiz.prompt: A late footstep feels wrong because
options: Sync with the picture is off
quiz.why: The impact should meet the visible step.

cards.title: Silence is a sound
cards.body: A sudden drop in ambience is as loud as a bang. The audience leans in because the room they trusted just disappeared. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: Room tone
cards.body: True digital zero can feel like a technical hole. A very low room tone under a quiet scene keeps the space alive without crowding the words.

cards.title: Before the hit
cards.body: Pull sound down just before a revelation or a scare. The contrast makes the next noise, or the continued quiet, feel larger. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Subjective silence
cards.body: After a blast, a ringing hush can put us in a character's ears. Bring the world back slowly as they recover. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Do not fear the pause
cards.body: A line that sits in quiet has edges. Filling every gap with music tells the audience what to feel and removes their work. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Endings
cards.body: Ending a scene on a held quiet can be stronger than a musical button. Let the last look finish before the next ambience arrives. Keep a one-line note so you can find the pattern again tomorrow.

quiz.prompt: A sudden silence works because of
options: Contrast with the sound before it
quiz.why: The drop is felt against what came before.

quiz.prompt: A little room tone under quiet scenes
options: Keeps the space from feeling like a dead hole
quiz.why: Low ambience maintains the room.

quiz.prompt: Subjective silence can follow
options: A loud blast in the character's ears
quiz.why: Ringing hush places us inside the impact.

cards.title: Clarity first
cards.body: If the audience cannot parse the words, the performance does not exist for them. Clarity is the first job, style comes after the sentence is understood.

cards.title: Breath and pace
cards.body: Keep the breaths that show thought. Remove the ones that are only noise between clean words. The edit of air is part of the performance. Look for the opposite choice in the following scene and compare the feeling.

cards.title: Overlaps
cards.body: People interrupt. A little overlap feels alive. Too much and both lines die. Choose whose words must win and duck the other gently. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Alternate takes
cards.body: You can build one reading from several takes if the room and the eyeline agree. A sudden change in distance or accent will show the seam.

cards.title: ADR with care
cards.body: Replacing a line later can save a noisy take. Match the energy and the distance. A booth voice in a shouty street scene sounds like a different room because it is.

cards.title: Offscreen lines
cards.body: A line from someone just outside the frame can carry a scene, but the picture still needs a place for us to look, usually the listener.

quiz.prompt: The first job of dialogue editing is
quiz.why: If the line cannot be understood, nothing else matters.

quiz.prompt: Overlapping speech should be
options: Controlled so the important words survive
quiz.why: A little overlap feels human. Too much hides both lines.

quiz.prompt: ADR fails when the new line
options: Sounds like a different room and energy
quiz.why: Booth recordings must agree with the photographed space.

cards.title: Cue the change
cards.body: Music is powerful when it marks a change: a decision, a memory, a turn into danger. If it plays under everything, it marks nothing. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: Enter quietly
cards.body: Bring a cue in under a breath or a look, not always on the cut. An entrance that is felt a second later can seem like the character's realization.

cards.title: Leave room for words
cards.body: Score and dialogue occupy the same attention. Thin the music, or choose a register that does not sit on the voice, when the line carries the plot.

cards.title: Source versus score
cards.body: A song from a car radio can be diegetic and still emotional. Know whether the character chose it. That choice is character, not just soundtrack. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Against the picture
cards.body: Cheerful music over a cruel image, used honestly, can be chilling or comic. The contrast is the point. Do not do it by accident. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Outro
cards.body: End the cue when the idea ends. A tail that drags into the next scene glues two ideas you may have wanted separate. Silence can be the cut.

quiz.prompt: Music communicates most clearly when it
options: Plays at one level for the entire film with no shape
quiz.why: A cue should have a reason to begin.

quiz.prompt: Under dialogue, music often needs to
options: Sit out of the way of the voice
quiz.why: The line has to remain understandable.

quiz.prompt: A song the character chose on a radio is
quiz.why: Source music can express taste and mood from inside the story.

cards.title: Hierarchy
cards.body: The mix decides what the audience hears first. Usually the voice leads, then story effects, then ambience and music. The order can change when the story asks.

cards.title: Depth
cards.body: Closer sounds are drier and more present. Farther sounds have more space around them. A shout from down the hall should not feel like a whisper in the ear.

cards.title: Perspective cuts
cards.body: When you cut from a wide shot to a close-up, the voice can come slightly nearer. A huge jump in tone between angles feels like two different recordings.

cards.title: Panning
cards.body: A little pan can follow a car or a person crossing. Hard left-right pans on ordinary dialogue become tiring and fight the center image. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Dynamic range
cards.body: Whispers and shouts need a path between them. If everything is equally loud, nothing can rise. Leave headroom so a slam can actually slam. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Check small speakers
cards.body: Play the mix on a laptop or a phone speaker as well as good headphones. If the words vanish, the mix only worked in the room where you made it.

quiz.prompt: In a typical dialogue scene the first priority is
quiz.why: Words usually lead the hierarchy.

quiz.prompt: Farther sounds should feel
quiz.why: Distance adds space and reduces intimacy.

quiz.prompt: Checking on a small speaker reveals whether
quiz.why: A mix that only works on big speakers will fail many viewers.

cards.title: A shape, not a cage
cards.body: Structure is the order of pressure. Someone wants something, an obstacle answers, and the situation changes. The labels you use matter less than the change. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: Beginning
cards.body: The opening shows the world and the want, or the lack of one. By the time the first turn arrives, we should know who we are following and why today is not ordinary.

cards.title: Middle
cards.body: The middle tests the want. Plans fail, alliances shift, and the person learns the real size of the problem. If nothing is harder at the halfway point, the story is idling.

cards.title: End
cards.body: The end forces a choice that costs something. A victory with no cost, or a loss with no meaning, both feel like the film stopped rather than concluded.

cards.title: Scenes are mini stories
cards.body: Each scene can have a small want and a small result. The result should make the next scene necessary. String those results and you have a plot.

cards.title: Outline in sentences
cards.body: Write the film as a chain of therefore and but, not and then. Therefore means consequence. But means reversal. And then is just a list. Keep a one-line note so you can find the pattern again tomorrow.

quiz.prompt: A useful story change requires
quiz.why: Pressure comes from desire meeting resistance.

quiz.prompt: The middle should generally make the problem
quiz.why: Tests escalate or reveal the real conflict.

quiz.prompt: Therefore and but are stronger than and then because they show
quiz.why: Causal links beat a loose list of events.

cards.title: Want versus need
cards.body: The want is what the person thinks will fix life. The need is what would actually change them. Stories get interesting when those two are not the same.

cards.title: Visible want
cards.body: A want you can photograph is stronger than a mood. Get the key, leave the town, win the apology, keep the secret. The audience can track a concrete aim.

cards.title: Opposition
cards.body: Someone or something should want the opposite, or want the same thing exclusively. Without opposition, the want is a walk, not a story. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Stakes
cards.body: Ask what happens if they fail today, not only at the end of the movie. Immediate stakes keep a scene from becoming a chat about a future problem.

cards.title: Change the want
cards.body: People can want a new thing after they learn. The change should come from an event, not from the writer getting bored of the old goal.

cards.title: Ensemble
cards.body: If several people want things, give each want a collision with the others. Parallel hobbies that never meet are two films sharing a poster. Keep a one-line note so you can find the pattern again tomorrow.

quiz.prompt: A photographable want is useful because the audience can
options: Track whether it is closer or farther
quiz.why: Concrete aims show progress and failure.

quiz.prompt: Opposition turns a wish into
quiz.why: Resistance creates drama.

quiz.prompt: Scene stakes should be
quiz.why: Today's risk keeps the scene alive.

cards.title: One job
cards.body: Before you write a scene, say what must be different at the end. If you cannot, the scene may be a corridor between real scenes. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: Enter with a tactic
cards.body: The person should try something: persuade, sneak, confess, stall, accuse. The tactic can fail. Watching a tactic is more alive than watching a topic. Look for the opposite choice in the following scene and compare the feeling.

cards.title: Turn
cards.body: Somewhere the balance shifts. New information, a refusal, a kiss, a threat. After the turn, the next action cannot be the same as the first one.

cards.title: Subtext welcome
cards.body: The goal can hide under small talk. Two people discussing coffee can really be negotiating a breakup, if the tactics and the turn are there. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Cut the throat clearing
cards.body: Greetings, repeated plans, and reminders of facts the audience knows are often the first lines to lose. Start at the tactic. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Exit on the new problem
cards.body: End when the goal is won, lost, or changed. The last line or look should make us need the following scene. Keep a one-line note so you can find the pattern again tomorrow.

quiz.prompt: A scene without a change at the end is often
quiz.why: Scenes exist to alter the situation.

quiz.prompt: A tactic is
options: What the person tries in order to get the goal
The color of the key light
quiz.why: We watch an attempt, not only a subject.

quiz.prompt: Ending on a new problem helps because
quiz.why: A fresh imbalance pulls us forward.

cards.title: Subtext
cards.body: Subtext is the meaning under the spoken words. People say they are fine while asking to be followed. The audience hears both layers when the picture helps.

cards.title: Do not write the theme out loud
cards.body: If a character explains the moral in a speech, the scene may be doing the audience's work. Let behavior carry the idea and keep the speech for pressure.

cards.title: Objects
cards.body: A character who keeps folding a letter is talking about the letter even if the dialogue is about dinner. The prop is a second sentence. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Contradiction
cards.body: The richest lines disagree with the face or the action. A smile while locking a door says more than a paragraph about trust. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Status
cards.body: Who sits, who stands, who pours the drink: status is subtext you can block. The words can pretend to be equal while the bodies are not.

cards.title: Trust the audience
cards.body: You do not need to cut to a flashback every time a line has a hidden meaning. If the situation is clear, the audience will do the math.

quiz.prompt: Subtext is
quiz.why: The spoken line and the real intent can differ.

quiz.prompt: A prop can act as subtext when
options: The handling says what the dialogue avoids
It is out of focus by mistake
quiz.why: Behavior with an object can be the real line.

quiz.prompt: Status can be shown by
options: Who sits, stands, or controls the room
quiz.why: Blocking reveals power even when the words sound polite.

cards.title: People do not write essays
cards.body: Spoken lines are shorter, more repetitive, and more evasive than prose. Read the scene aloud. Anywhere you run out of breath, the line is still written, not spoken.

cards.title: Distinct mouths
cards.body: A formal person and a blunt person should not share the same sentence shape. Vocabulary, rhythm, and what they refuse to say are character. Look for the opposite choice in the following scene and compare the feeling.

cards.title: On the nose
cards.body: On-the-nose dialogue says the emotion and the plot directly. Sometimes a crisis needs that clarity. Most of the time, aim beside the target and let behavior finish the thought.

cards.title: Questions
cards.body: A scene of mutual interviewing can feel like a form. Mix questions with attempts, jokes, and refusals so the talk has tactics. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Silence in the script
cards.body: Write the pause. A beat where someone does not answer is dialogue. Do not fill it just because the page looks empty. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Last line
cards.body: The last line of a scene should turn the screw or release it. A trailing pleasantry often means you have not found the end yet. Keep a one-line note so you can find the pattern again tomorrow.

quiz.prompt: A practical test for spoken dialogue is to
quiz.why: Breath and rhythm reveal written lines.

quiz.prompt: On-the-nose dialogue
options: States emotion and plot too directly
quiz.why: It says the subtext out loud.

quiz.prompt: A written pause is
quiz.why: Not answering is still a dramatic action.

cards.title: The job of a logline
cards.body: A logline is one or two sentences that hold a protagonist, a goal, an obstacle, and the stakes. It is a compass, not a trailer full of twists.

cards.title: Protagonist
cards.body: Name the kind of person, not a list of traits. A cautious archivist is more useful than someone who is nice, smart, and brave. Look for the opposite choice in the following scene and compare the feeling.

cards.title: Goal and obstacle
cards.body: The goal should be active. The obstacle should be strong enough that success is uncertain. If the obstacle is only bad luck for one minute, the story is thin.

cards.title: Stakes
cards.body: Stakes say what is lost if the goal fails. Keep them concrete: the building, the alibi, the last chance to speak. Vague sadness is harder to film.

cards.title: No ending spoiler
cards.body: The logline should open the question, not answer it. If your sentence includes the final choice, you wrote a summary of the last act. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Length
cards.body: Aim for roughly twenty-five to forty words. If it is longer, you are probably telling scenes. If it is shorter, you may be missing the obstacle or the cost.

quiz.prompt: A logline should include
quiz.why: Those four parts aim the story.

quiz.prompt: The ending should usually stay
quiz.why: The sentence should open a question.

quiz.prompt: A useful length is about
quiz.why: Enough for the four parts, not a treatment.

cards.title: Blocking
cards.body: Blocking is the planned path of bodies in the space. It decides who is near, who is trapped, and when a crossing changes the power. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: Geography first
cards.body: Know the doors, the table, and the window before you invent poses. People move because the room offers choices, not because the page says they cross.

cards.title: Triangles
cards.body: Three people in a triangle keep everyone visible and give you a strong and a weak position. A straight line of faces is harder to cover and flatter to watch.

cards.title: Approach and retreat
cards.body: Stepping closer is pressure. Stepping back is refusal or fear. Let the distance change when the tactic changes, not on a random line. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Business
cards.body: Give hands a job: pouring, folding, fixing a latch. Business reveals nerves and also gives the editor matches. Empty hands often look like waiting for the next line.

cards.title: Marks with mercy
cards.body: Marks help the camera, but actors need a reason to land on them. Tie the stop to a look, a touch, or an object so the movement feels caused.

quiz.prompt: Blocking is the plan for
options: How people move through the space
quiz.why: Paths and positions are the blocking.

quiz.prompt: A triangle of three people helps
quiz.why: The shape keeps faces readable and status clear.

quiz.prompt: Crossing closer usually reads as
quiz.why: Distance is emotional as well as physical.

cards.title: What coverage is
cards.body: Coverage is the set of angles that will let the scene be cut. A master, singles, and a detail are a common kit. Shoot what the story needs, not every side of the room.

cards.title: The master
cards.body: The master shows the geography and the full action. Even if you think you will live in close-ups, the master saves you when the close-ups do not cut.

cards.title: Singles
cards.body: A single is one person. Matching lens and eyeline across singles keeps the conversation in one world. Wild changes in size make the edit hiccup. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Inserts
cards.body: Shoot the hand, the key, the phone, while the light still matches. Inserts are cheap on set and expensive to fake later. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Safety and risk
cards.body: Get a safe version that tells the story, then a braver version. If the day collapses, the safe version still makes a scene. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Shot list as a servant
cards.body: The list is a plan, not a vow. If a performance offers a better angle, change the list and protect the angles you still need for geography.

quiz.prompt: A master is useful because it
quiz.why: The wide view protects the cut.

quiz.prompt: An insert should be filmed
options: Next month in a new room
quiz.why: Matching light keeps the detail in the same world.

quiz.prompt: A safe take plus a braver take means
options: You can still cut the scene if the risk fails
quiz.why: Safety protects the story. The risk explores it.

cards.title: Why rehearse
cards.body: Rehearsal is where the scene stops being words and becomes behavior. You learn which lines are false and which crosses are only traffic. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: Table then floor
cards.body: Talk the intentions first, then stand up. Intentions without movement stay abstract. Movement without intentions becomes marching. Look for the opposite choice in the following scene and compare the feeling.

cards.title: Ask questions
cards.body: Ask what the person wants in the next ten seconds, not how to feel a general emotion. Specific wants produce specific actions. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Trim in the room
cards.body: If a line dies in the air, cut it in rehearsal while everyone can agree. Protecting a dead line until the edit wastes the day. Replay ten seconds and point at the exact moment the choice lands.

cards.title: Camera in the loop
cards.body: Once blocking works, walk the camera path. A beautiful cross that cannot be seen is not yet a shot. Adjust the path or the lens together.

cards.title: Leave a little unknown
cards.body: Over-rehearsing can polish the life out of a take. Stop when the shape is clear and one or two discoveries are still possible on camera. Keep a one-line note so you can find the pattern again tomorrow.

quiz.prompt: Rehearsal turns the page into
quiz.why: You test movement and intention before rolling.

quiz.prompt: A useful question is about
options: The want in the next moment
quiz.why: Immediate wants create playable actions.

quiz.prompt: Stop rehearsing when
options: The shape is clear but a little life remains
The words are memorized and the bodies are frozen
quiz.why: Leave room for a discovery on the take.

cards.title: Tone
cards.body: Tone is the attitude of the telling: comic, grave, tender, bleak, playful. It is a promise about how the audience should hold the events. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: Agreement
cards.body: Performance, lens, light, and cutting all vote. If the acting is broad and the cutting is funeral-slow, the votes disagree and the scene feels confused. Look for the opposite choice in the following scene and compare the feeling.

cards.title: Set the range early
cards.body: The opening scenes teach the audience how big the jokes and the dangers are. A sudden different size later can work as a turn, but not as an accident.

cards.title: Contrast inside the promise
cards.body: A grim story can have a kind joke if the joke belongs to a character. The joke should not wink at the audience and cancel the stakes.

cards.title: Talk in plain words
cards.body: On set, replace tone adjectives with actions. Instead of be more intense, ask for a quieter voice and a step closer. People can play actions. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Protect the turn
cards.body: If the tone shifts, mark the moment: a look, a silence, a change of light. An unmarked shift feels like a different movie wandered in. Keep a one-line note so you can find the pattern again tomorrow.

quiz.prompt: Tone is
options: The attitude of how the story is told
quiz.why: It is the stance the film takes toward events.

quiz.prompt: Departments should
options: Agree on the size of the feeling
quiz.why: Picture and performance vote together.

quiz.prompt: Direction is clearer when you ask for
options: Silence from the whole crew forever
quiz.why: Playable verbs beat abstract moods.

cards.title: A list is a map
cards.body: A shot list is the order of setups you intend to shoot, with the size and the purpose of each. It is how the day stays tied to the scene.

cards.title: Purpose column
cards.body: Next to each shot, write why it exists: geography, reaction, insert, reveal. If you cannot write the why, you may not need the setup. Look for the opposite choice in the following scene and compare the feeling.

cards.title: Order for light and energy
cards.body: Group setups that share a lighting state. Also consider performance energy. Sometimes you shoot the calm coverage before the shouting, so voices survive. Sketch a tiny frame in the margin and mark where the choice sits.

cards.title: Time truth
cards.body: Estimate honestly. A company move across the room is not free. A list that needs fourteen hours in a ten-hour day is a wish, not a plan.

cards.title: Must, should, could
cards.body: Mark the shots the scene dies without, the shots that make it good, and the shots that are gifts. When time slips, the gifts go first.

cards.title: Rewrite at lunch
cards.body: If the morning changed the scene, rewrite the afternoon list. Clinging to a dead plan produces coverage for a film you are no longer making. Keep a one-line note so you can find the pattern again tomorrow.

quiz.prompt: Each shot on the list should have
quiz.why: Purpose keeps the day tied to the cut.

quiz.prompt: When time runs short, drop
quiz.why: Must-have shots protect the story.

quiz.prompt: Grouping setups by light
options: Saves time and keeps the look consistent
quiz.why: Fewer relights mean more takes.

cards.title: One voice
cards.body: People need to know who can say action and who can stop the take. Multiple overlapping bosses create polite chaos and missed notes. Name the choice out loud the next time a scene uses it.

cards.title: Short notes
cards.body: Give one or two notes between takes, aimed at a person, tied to a moment. A speech about the whole film makes the next take worse, not better.

cards.title: Heads of department
cards.body: Talk to the camera, light, and sound leads before you change the plan. A surprise move wastes their work and the trust you need at the next surprise.

cards.title: Quiet near the frame
cards.body: The energy beside the lens leaks into the performance. If the set is chatty, the scene gets chatty. Call for quiet as a tool, not a scolding.

cards.title: Credit the crew
cards.body: When a suggestion saves the shot, say so. People protect a director who shares the win, and they hide problems from one who only blames. Ask what would change if the opposite choice replaced this one.

cards.title: Decide
cards.body: Gather the useful facts, then choose. Endless maybe is expensive. A clear choice, even a reversible one, lets the company move. Keep a one-line note so you can find the pattern again tomorrow.

quiz.prompt: Notes between takes work best when they are
options: Few and tied to a moment
A speech about the whole career
quiz.why: Specific, short notes can be played on the next take.

quiz.prompt: Changing the plan without telling department leads
quiz.why: Surprises in craft departments cost time.

quiz.prompt: A clear decision helps because
quiz.why: Action beats endless hesitation.

terms.title: Shot Size
terms.definition: Shot size is how much of the person and the place the frame includes. It runs from an extreme wide view, where a figure is small in a large world, to an extreme close-up of eyes or mouth. The size decides what information the audience can use.
terms.tip: If the place is the pressure, stay wider. If a lie or a blink is the pressure, come closer.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on distance and framing.

terms.title: Camera Angle
terms.definition: Camera angle is the height and tilt from which we see the subject. Eye level feels even. A low angle looks up and can enlarge power. A high angle looks down and can shrink it.
terms.tip: Pick the height after you decide who holds the moment.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on angle and power.

terms.title: Rule of Thirds
terms.definition: The rule of thirds divides the frame into a grid and parks important shapes near the crossings. Lead room is the open space in front of a look or a walk. Headroom is the air above the hair.
terms.tip: Settle on the grid when the move ends, and break it when symmetry is the point.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on thirds and lead room.

terms.title: Depth Layers
terms.definition: Depth layers are the foreground, the subject, and the background working together. A near shape such as a shoulder or doorway gives the eye a way in. Separation in light or focus keeps the person from melting into the wall.
terms.tip: One clear shape at each distance is enough. Clutter is not the same as depth.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on layers and space.

terms.title: Focal Length
terms.definition: Focal length describes how wide or narrow a lens sees. Short lenses take in more room and stretch distance. Long lenses isolate a slice and stack the background closer to the subject.
terms.tip: The same crop from a different distance is a different picture. Change lens and position together.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on lenses.

terms.title: Camera Move
terms.definition: A camera move travels or turns to follow attention. A pan swivels, a tilt tips, a dolly actually rolls, and a zoom only changes the lens. The move should begin for a story reason and end on a frame you could hold.
terms.tip: Ease in and ease out. A hard start looks like an accident.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on moving the camera.

terms.title: Three-Point Light
terms.definition: Three-point light is a working trio: key for shape, fill for shadow detail, and back light for a rim that separates the body from the set. The relationship between them matters more than the number of lamps.
terms.tip: Start with the key alone. Add fill or rim only when the picture asks.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on key, fill, and back.

terms.title: Hard and Soft Light
terms.definition: Hard light comes from a small source and throws a crisp shadow. Soft light comes from a large source relative to the face and wraps the features. Moving a soft source closer makes it softer still.
terms.tip: Read the nose shadow. A sharp stripe means the key is hard.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on hard and soft edges.

terms.title: Color Temperature
terms.definition: Color temperature is the warm or cool cast of a source. Lamps and sunset lean amber. Shade and many night windows lean blue. A warm face against a cool background separates without shouting.
terms.tip: Let the visible source motivate the color, and keep skin in a range you still believe.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on warm and cool light.

terms.title: Contrast Ratio
terms.definition: Contrast is the gap between bright and shadow. A small gap feels open. A large gap feels dramatic or secret. You can judge a face by squinting: if the shadow cheek vanishes, the gap is high.
terms.tip: Decide whether the eyes must survive the darkness before you crush the shadow.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on contrast.

terms.title: Motivated Light
terms.definition: Motivated light pretends to come from a cause in the story, such as a window, a lamp, or the sky. A practical is a lamp the camera can see. A hidden source may imitate it from the same side.
terms.tip: You can cheat a little toward the lens, but stay on the source's side of the face.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on cause and practicals.

terms.title: Lighting Mood
terms.definition: Lighting mood is the emotional word the light is aiming at: safe, lonely, harsh, tender, clinical. Direction, color, and contrast all vote. Coverage should keep that vote from setup to setup.
terms.tip: Replace vague mood talk with a direction, a color, and a contrast you can set.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on mood.

terms.title: Cut
terms.definition: A cut joins two shots at a chosen frame and reads as a thought: closer, later, meanwhile, or therefore. The best cuts answer a question or follow an action. A cut that adds nothing feels like a blink.
terms.tip: Cut on motion when you can, and stay on a reaction when the listener holds the story.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on cuts.

terms.title: Continuity
terms.definition: Continuity keeps trust in space and time. Screen direction, eyelines, and props should agree across a cut unless you show a turn. The imaginary line between people helps their left and right stay stable.
terms.tip: Break continuity only when the style announces the break, as in a dream or a panic.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on continuity.

terms.title: Editing Rhythm
terms.definition: Editing rhythm is the pattern of shot lengths. Short shots hurry. Long holds wait. An accent is a length that breaks the pattern so a beat can land. Music can ride that pattern or push against it.
terms.tip: Watch the scene without sound. If the pulse disappears, the picture was not carrying it.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on rhythm.

terms.title: Montage
terms.definition: A montage compresses a stretch of time into a chain of fragments. Each fragment should show change, and the sequence should land on a clear after. One song, voice, or repeated gesture can glue the days together.
terms.tip: Do not hide leftover shots in a montage. If a shot does not change the state, cut it.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on montage.

terms.title: Transition
terms.definition: A transition is how one shot or scene hands off to the next. Straight cuts do most of the work. Dissolves and fades suggest time or chapters. A match cut compares two shapes. Sound can lead the picture across the join.
terms.tip: Use a fancy transition only when you want it to be noticed.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on transitions.

terms.title: Pacing
terms.definition: Pacing is how quickly story information arrives. Enter scenes late, leave when the decision has landed, and let a pause give weight. Pace is relative: a fast scene feels faster after a slow one.
terms.tip: Build the film as a series of breaths, not one speed from start to finish.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on pacing.

terms.title: Diegetic Sound
terms.definition: Diegetic sound belongs to the story world, such as footsteps or a radio the characters could hear. Non-diegetic sound, such as a traditional score, is for the audience alone. A song can cross that border if the handoff is clear.
terms.tip: Ask who in the scene can hear it. That answer sorts the layer.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on story sound and score.

terms.title: Foley
terms.definition: Foley is movement sound performed to picture: steps, cloth, and object handling. Dialogue microphones often miss those details. The surface under a shoe tells us where we are, and sync must meet the visible impact.
terms.tip: Add the gestures that carry story and leave the rest quiet.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on foley.

terms.title: Silence
terms.definition: Silence in a mix is a deliberate drop, usually against sound that came before. A little room tone keeps a quiet scene from feeling like a dead technical hole. Subjective silence, such as ringing after a blast, puts us in a character's ears.
terms.tip: Pull level down before a revelation if you want the next moment to feel larger.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on silence.

terms.title: Dialogue Edit
terms.definition: Dialogue editing makes words understandable and keeps the breaths that show thought. Small overlaps feel alive. Replacement lines must match the energy and the room or they will sound like a different place.
terms.tip: Clarity comes first. Style that hides the sentence has not finished the job.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on dialogue editing.

terms.title: Music Cue
terms.definition: A music cue marks a change: a decision, a memory, a turn. It should enter with a reason, leave room for words, and end when the idea ends. A song a character chooses is also character, not only decoration.
terms.tip: If the cue plays under everything, it stops meaning anything.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on music cues.

terms.title: Sound Mix
terms.definition: The mix sets hierarchy, distance, and loudness. Voices usually lead, close sounds feel dry, and far sounds have more space. Leave room so a loud hit can rise. Then check the words on a small speaker.
terms.tip: A huge jump in voice tone between a wide shot and a close-up feels like two rooms.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on the mix.

terms.title: Story Structure
terms.definition: Story structure is the order of pressure: a want, an obstacle, and a change. Openings show the want, middles test it, and endings force a choice that costs something. Therefore and but are stronger links than and then.
terms.tip: Each scene can be a small story whose result makes the next scene necessary.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on story shape.

terms.title: Character Desire
terms.definition: Desire is what a person is trying to get. A want you can photograph is easier to track than a mood. Opposition and immediate stakes turn the want into drama. The deeper need may not match the want.
terms.tip: If several people want things, let those wants collide.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on desire.

terms.title: Scene Goal
terms.definition: A scene goal is the change that must happen before the scene ends. The person tries a tactic, the balance turns, and the exit leaves a new problem. Talk can hide the goal, but the goal still has to be there.
terms.tip: If nothing is different at the end, you may have written a corridor.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on scene goals.

terms.title: Subtext
terms.definition: Subtext is the meaning under the words. Props, contradictions, and status in the blocking can say what the dialogue avoids. Trust the audience to do the math when the situation is clear.
terms.tip: A speech that explains the moral often replaces behavior the scene could have shown.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on subtext.

terms.title: Dialogue
terms.definition: Dialogue is speech shaped like talk: short, evasive, and full of different rhythms. Read it aloud. On-the-nose lines say the feeling directly. A pause can be a line. The last line should turn or release the scene.
terms.tip: Give each person a different sentence shape so their mouths are not interchangeable.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on dialogue.

terms.title: Logline
terms.definition: A logline is one or two sentences with a protagonist, a goal, an obstacle, and the stakes. It should open the question rather than spoil the ending. A useful length is about twenty-five to forty words.
terms.tip: If the sentence is a list of scenes, it is no longer a compass.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on loglines.

terms.title: Blocking
terms.definition: Blocking is the path of bodies in a space: who approaches, who retreats, and where people stop. Triangles keep faces visible. Distance changes when tactics change. Hands need a job so the movement looks caused.
terms.tip: Tie a mark to a look or an object so the actor is not marching to tape.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on blocking.

terms.title: Coverage
terms.definition: Coverage is the set of angles that lets a scene be cut: often a master, singles, and inserts. The master protects geography. Inserts should match the light. A safe version plus a braver version keeps the day alive.
terms.tip: Write why each shot exists. If you cannot, you may not need the setup.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on coverage.

terms.title: Rehearsal
terms.definition: Rehearsal turns the page into behavior. Talk about the immediate want, then walk the space, then check that the camera can see the path. Cut dead lines in the room. Stop before the life is polished away.
terms.tip: Ask what the person wants in the next ten seconds, not how to feel in general.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on rehearsal.

terms.title: Tone
terms.definition: Tone is the attitude of the telling. Performance, light, lens, and cutting should agree on how big the feelings are. Shifts in tone need a marked moment or they feel like a different film wandered in.
terms.tip: On set, replace tone adjectives with actions a person can play.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on tone.

terms.title: Shot List
terms.definition: A shot list orders the setups and states the purpose of each. Group work that shares a lighting state. Mark what the scene must have and what is only a gift. Rewrite the list when the scene changes.
terms.tip: A list that needs more hours than the day has is a wish.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on shot lists.

terms.title: Set Communication
terms.definition: Set communication is how decisions and quiet move through the company. One person calls the take. Notes stay short. Department leads hear plan changes. A clear choice lets everyone move.
terms.tip: Praise a save out loud. People protect a set where credit is shared.
terms.unlock: Pass the lesson on talking on set.

terms.title: Rack Focus
terms.definition: A rack focus shifts sharpness from one plane to another during the shot, handing attention from a near face to a far door or the reverse. The shift itself is the cut, done inside one image.
terms.tip: Motivate the shift with a look or a sound so it feels noticed by someone.
terms.unlock: Unlocks when a streak reaches 3 days.

terms.title: Jump Cut
terms.definition: A jump cut joins two similar angles and drops a piece of time, so the person seems to blink forward. It can feel comic, anxious, or modern. In a classical scene it reads as a mistake unless the style wants the jump.
terms.tip: Use it when time itself is the feeling, not when you are hiding a flub.
terms.unlock: Unlocks when a streak reaches 7 days.

terms.title: Match Cut
terms.definition: A match cut joins two shots through a similar shape, motion, or idea, such as a round window becoming a round plate. The audience feels the comparison before they can explain it.
terms.tip: The match should say something, not only look clever.
terms.unlock: Unlocks when a streak reaches 14 days.

terms.title: Chiaroscuro
terms.definition: Chiaroscuro is a strong pattern of light and dark, with deep shadow and a bright edge of form. Faces become sculpted. The mood often feels period, secret, or severe.
terms.tip: Keep one readable feature, usually the eyes, so the portrait does not turn into a pure silhouette.
terms.unlock: Unlocks when a streak reaches 30 days.

terms.title: Dolly Zoom
terms.definition: A dolly zoom moves the camera nearer while zooming out, or farther while zooming in, so the subject stays a similar size and the background breathes. The world warps while the person holds still. It often marks a realization or a dread.
terms.tip: Use it rarely. A trick this visible needs a mental shift to justify it.
terms.unlock: Unlocks when a streak reaches 60 days.

terms.title: Cold Open
terms.definition: A cold open starts the story before titles or ordinary setup, often in the middle of a problem. It promises tone and stakes quickly, then lets the film widen.
terms.tip: Do not explain the cold open with a later speech. Let the images keep their lead.
terms.unlock: Unlocks when a streak reaches 100 days.

terms.title: MacGuffin
terms.definition: A MacGuffin is an object or goal everyone chases whose exact nature matters less than the chase. The case, the letter, or the prototype pushes people into conflict. The drama lives in what they will do to get it.
terms.tip: Give the object clear stakes even if its inner workings stay vague.
terms.unlock: Unlocks at the Clapper Loader rank.

terms.title: Dutch Angle
terms.definition: A Dutch angle rolls the camera so the horizon tilts. Verticals lean. The frame feels unstable, intoxicated, or menacing. A slight tilt reads as an error. A clear tilt reads as style.
terms.tip: Return to level when the unease should pass, or the whole film will feel accidentally crooked.
terms.unlock: Unlocks at the Editor rank.

terms.title: Eyeline
terms.definition: An eyeline is the direction a person looks, and where that look lands in the next shot. Matched eyelines convince us two people see each other. A missed eyeline makes them look past one another.
terms.tip: If you cut to what they see, the angle of the look should agree with the angle of the object.
terms.unlock: Unlocks at the Director rank.

terms.title: Practical Light
terms.definition: A practical is a visible lamp, screen, or window light that belongs to the set. It may need help from a hidden source that copies its direction and color. The audience believes the glow they can see.
terms.tip: Dim the practical bulb so it looks real on camera instead of a white blob.
terms.unlock: Unlocks after three perfect spotting rounds.

terms.title: L-Cut
terms.definition: An L-cut lets the sound of one shot continue under the picture of the next, or brings the next sound in early. Conversation feels smoother because words are not trapped inside a single face.
terms.tip: Use it so we watch the listener while the speaker finishes.
terms.unlock: Unlocks after a framing score of 95 or more.

terms.title: Insert Shot
terms.definition: An insert is a close detail of an object that the wider shots cannot read: a key, a name on paper, a ticking hand. It answers a question. Shoot it in matching light so it belongs to the scene.
terms.tip: Hold the insert long enough to read, then get out.
terms.unlock: Unlocks after 10 diary entries.

briefs.detail: Keep the subject high, with only a little air above the head.

briefs.detail: Center the subject and keep the horizon quiet behind them.
